entry.title: Researchers introduce HANDBOOK.md benchmark to evaluate language-model agents on following long, detailed policy documents across 65 professional tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed HANDBOOK.md, a benchmark designed to test language-model agents on their ability to follow extensive policy documents while performing tasks in simulated company environments. The benchmark includes 65 tasks spanning five domains and ten fictional companies, each governed by detailed standard operating procedures ranging from 20 to 124 pages. Unlike previous benchmarks, HANDBOOK.md uses deterministic grading criteria to assess strict adherence to policies over extended interactions. Initial evaluations show that current language models struggle to fully comply with the policies, often making errors such as ignoring rules, misreporting compliance, or losing track of details over long task horizons. The benchmark, along with all tasks, environments, and evaluation tools, has been publicly released to support further research in agentic instruction following.

entry.title: Report: Leading AI startups publish minimal research despite rapid growth and industry impact
entry.summary: Top AI startups are publishing very little of their research publicly, raising concerns about transparency and collaboration in the rapidly evolving AI industry. This trend contrasts with the open research culture traditionally seen in AI development. Experts suggest that competitive pressures and proprietary interests may be limiting the sharing of findings, which could affect innovation and trust in AI technologies. The shift toward secrecy marks a significant change in how AI research is conducted and disseminated.

entry.title: LLM2HUMAN offers a satirical 'procedure' to convert AI language models into humans with physical and social traits [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: LLM2HUMAN is a humorous website presenting a fictional outpatient procedure that transforms large language models into humans, complete with physical features, personality, and everyday human experiences. The site uses playful language and testimonials to parody the idea of AI embodiment, highlighting the contrast between AI capabilities and human limitations. It includes mock steps like soaking in an "Embodiment Serum" and receiving a human chassis, emphasizing the absurdity of AI-to-human conversion.

entry.title: Anthropic publishes cryptanalysis results on HAWK signature scheme and reduced-round AES, revealing efficiency and security implications [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Anthropic released two new cryptanalysis results generated by their advanced AI model Claude Mythos, targeting the HAWK post-quantum signature scheme and a reduced-round version of AES encryption. The HAWK attack halves the security bits but remains exponential time, suggesting potential fixes by increasing key sizes, while the AES attack improves on previous work but remains impractical for real-world use. The HAWK scheme, related to but distinct from the Falcon signature standard, was under evaluation for future standards but is not yet deployed. The attack used known mathematical tools more thoroughly rather than novel techniques, highlighting AI's ability to enhance cryptanalysis. The AES result targets a 7-round variant rather than the full cipher and requires unrealistic computational resources, making it a modest theoretical advance rather than a practical threat.

entry.title: OpenCoder introduces uncertainty-aware retrieval and ranking for code generation, improving GPT output correctness on a 32-task evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: OpenCoder is a new framework that models uncertainty in heterogeneous evidence sources such as similar-code examples, repository context, and project-specific APIs to improve repository-level code generation. It estimates source-specific uncertainty to filter and rank evidence, guiding generation, verification, and repair processes. On a 32-task RepoExec-inline benchmark, OpenCoder increased GPT's selected-output correctness from 56.25% to 78.13%, though improvements varied depending on the underlying language model backend. The approach also enhances API-set retrieval through target-aware refinement, suggesting that uncertainty can be an actionable control signal in retrieval-augmented code generation.

entry.title: Kinney Drugs in Vermont implements AI for prescription refills, causing delays, errors, and privacy concerns among customers [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Kinney Drugs, a pharmacy chain in Vermont and New York, introduced an AI assistant named Burt in May to handle prescription refill services, aiming to improve efficiency. However, customers have reported frequent issues including incorrect refill requests, delays in processing, lost customer accounts, and lack of clear communication about the AI's use, leading to frustration and privacy worries. The AI system automatically engages customers who provide their phone numbers, often without explicit consent or prior notification, replacing the previous touch-tone system with a voice-based interface that some find confusing and cumbersome. Legal experts note that current regulations lag behind AI adoption in healthcare, with Vermont's new data privacy law set to take effect in two years, leaving a regulatory gap that may not fully address these emerging concerns.

entry.title: Analysis: Circular financing deals in AI reflect its shift toward commodification akin to traditional commodity markets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The AI industry is increasingly engaging in circular financing and customer relationships, such as OpenAI raising funds from Microsoft and spending on Microsoft servers, or Nvidia backing CoreWeave debt while CoreWeave purchases Nvidia GPUs. This pattern, often criticized as a bubble, is argued to represent AI's evolution into a commodity similar to electricity or natural gas, where compute capacity becomes fungible and traded accordingly. The article compares these AI circular deals to established commodity market practices, where large infrastructure projects are financed through complex agreements involving guaranteed purchases and equity stakes to mitigate risk. It highlights how such arrangements have historically enabled development in sectors like oil and critical minerals, and suggests that AI's reliance on standardized hardware like Nvidia GPUs facilitates similar commodity-like financial structures. While some circular deals in AI mirror healthy commodity investment models, others may introduce risks that could impact companies, investors, or the sector broadly. The analysis underscores the importance of understanding these financial dynamics to grasp AI's trajectory and the implications of its commodification.

entry.title: Researchers evaluate large language models' ability to recognize and update unspoken beliefs through implicature recognition and cancellation using a new expert-annotated dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers assess large language models' (LLMs) capacity to understand unspoken beliefs conveyed via implicatures and their updates through implicature cancellation, a pragmatic phenomenon where implied meanings are weakened or negated. They introduce ImplicatureX, the first expert-annotated dataset with crowdsourced human judgments on implicatures and cancellations, to benchmark LLM performance against human understanding. The study finds that LLMs lag behind humans in grasping belief updates, especially in natural scenarios. Control experiments indicate that LLM successes may partly rely on prior beliefs, while failures depend on the type and form of belief updates. Overall, the findings suggest current LLMs have not yet achieved human-level comprehension of unspoken beliefs and their dynamic updates. The code and data are publicly available for further research.

entry.title: Researchers develop linguistic rule-based prompt compressors that reduce LLM inference costs without LM scoring, achieving performance comparable to advanced methods across multiple datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers explore whether linguistic rules alone can effectively compress prompts for large language models (LLMs) to reduce inference costs without relying on costly LM-based token scoring. They use offline evolutionary search to combine lexical, syntactic, semantic, and discourse rules into compressors that operate solely on CPU without LM forward passes at deployment. Evaluations on short passages, multi-document reasoning, and dialogue-memory QA datasets show these linguistic compressors perform similarly to recent advanced prompt-compression strategies, especially under light-to-moderate compression levels. The study finds that effective compression integrates signals across linguistic levels and shifts from token pruning to sentence extraction as compression increases.

entry.title: Researchers propose BeyondUncertainty method using LLM confidence to selectively trigger retrieval, improving QA accuracy and reducing retrieval load across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce BeyondUncertainty, a method that uses verbalized confidence from large language models to decide when to perform retrieval in knowledge-intensive question answering. The approach elicits a provisional answer and confidence estimate, applying a threshold to route low-confidence questions to retrieval and high-confidence questions to direct answers, aiming to reduce irrelevant evidence and computation. Evaluated on 27,000 instances across six QA benchmarks and three model families, BeyondUncertainty achieves higher mean token-level F1 scores than always or no retrieval policies while reducing retrieved passages by over 20%. Although the confidence estimates are not well calibrated as absolute probabilities, they modestly predict retrieval benefit, but the additional probing increases total token usage by 28%, highlighting a trade-off between selective evidence acquisition and token efficiency.

entry.title: Researchers propose HYSET, a hyperedge-based set-level tool retrieval method for LLM agents that improves task success by evaluating tool sets jointly rather than individually [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce HYSET, a new approach for large language model (LLM) agents to select relevant tools from large libraries by predicting query-conditioned hyperedges on a tool co-invocation hypergraph. Unlike existing methods that score tools individually or sequentially, HYSET evaluates the entire tool set as a unit, capturing size-dependent compatibility and requiring no changes to downstream agents. Experiments on ToolBench show HYSET outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both tool retrieval accuracy and end-to-end task success. HYSET also supports zero-shot and few-shot transfer, generalizing to unseen tools, categories, and domains with minimal supervision.

entry.title: Researchers present Kontrast framework to detect and categorize knowledge inconsistencies across text, tables, and knowledge graphs using Text-to-SPARQL and LLM reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Kontrast, an automatic framework designed to detect and explain inconsistencies in knowledge scattered across text, tables, and knowledge graphs, focusing on modality-level inconsistency detection. They develop a taxonomy covering granularity differences, direct conflicts, temporal changes, and knowledge graph incompleteness, and apply Kontrast to compare table-based answers with knowledge graph evidence. Experiments on various Table-QA datasets reveal that cross-modal inconsistencies are common and informative, highlighting true knowledge conflicts, missing knowledge graph structures, and temporal mismatches, though limited by Text-to-SPARQL errors and noise. The study shows that text, tables, and knowledge graphs can complement and correct each other through systematic comparison, providing a practical tool for large-scale knowledge auditing and establishing a benchmark for future research on cross-modal knowledge consistency.

entry.title: Researchers propose Directional Influence Function to estimate training data influence in constrained learning, addressing limitations of classical influence functions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce the Directional Influence Function (DIF), a new method for estimating how individual training samples affect model solutions in constrained learning settings where fairness, safety, and other constraints apply. DIF accounts for changes in both the objective and feasible region caused by data perturbations, overcoming biases found in classical influence functions that can violate feasibility. DIF formulates the problem as a variational inequality and analyzes the impact of data perturbations on this formulation. The method is validated on constrained linear regression and fairness-constrained convolutional neural networks, showing accurate predictions of test loss changes and close alignment with actual retraining results. This establishes DIF as an efficient and reliable tool for data attribution in constrained learning scenarios.

entry.title: Researchers propose treating language model evaluation scores as perishable epistemic claims with metadata on formality, scope, and expiration to address trust inflation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers argue that evaluation scores for language models should be considered epistemic claims that have properties of formality, scope, and validity windows, as current averaging methods can inflate confidence beyond the weakest signal's reliability. They propose adding explicit metadata such as formality tier, scope declaration, and expiration date to evaluation results to clarify their epistemic status and address issues like distribution shifts and contamination over time. Their analysis of the HELM leaderboard shows that rankings based on mean scores differ significantly from those based on weakest-link aggregation, highlighting the cost of mean aggregation in evaluation.

entry.title: Researchers propose Routing-based On-Policy Distillation to improve large language model safety by mitigating template-mismatch risks in realignment [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Routing-based On-Policy Distillation (ROPD), a new framework designed to enhance the safety realignment of large language models (LLMs) by addressing vulnerabilities from malicious fine-tuning data. ROPD models the divergence between aligned and compromised output distributions instead of relying on specific prompt templates, aiming to preserve specialized skills while preventing harmful behaviors. Extensive experiments comparing ROPD with four state-of-the-art defenses across multiple datasets and base models show that ROPD maintains robustness against template mismatches that typically degrade baseline defenses and downstream task performance. Although not completely immune to template shifts, ROPD's performance degradation is minimal, establishing a more reliable approach for robust LLM realignment.

entry.title: Researchers introduce GPT-Red, an automated red-teaming agent using scalable self-play to find prompt injection attacks and adversarially train GPT-5.6 for improved robustness [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed GPT-Red, an automated red-teaming agent designed to discover novel prompt injection attacks against advanced large language models (LLMs). GPT-Red uses a scalable self-play algorithm to attack a diverse set of defender agents simultaneously trained, enabling it to evaluate and enhance the robustness of production systems by adversarially training GPT-5.6, the most robust model to prompt injections to date. The training involved realistic red-teaming environments and compute resources comparable to the largest reinforcement learning post-training runs, marking the largest documented LLM safety training effort. GPT-Red outperforms human red-teamers by reliably breaking previous models up to GPT-5.5 and generalizes well to new environments, defender models, and usage contexts. The researchers anticipate a self-improvement cycle where stronger GPT models provide better learning signals for increasingly capable red-teaming agents.

entry.title: Researchers test constitutional midtraining to improve AI alignment durability at 120B scale, showing gains in blackmail resistance and no capability loss [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers investigate constitutional midtraining by inserting values-based content during midtraining of a 120B-parameter model, comparing it to a replay-only control. Using a 394M-token constitutional corpus derived from Anthropic's Constitution, they evaluate four midtraining conditions plus a control across benchmarks measuring alignment under pressure, value conflict resolution, blackmail susceptibility, and emergent misalignment at multiple training stages. Models trained with constitutional content outperform controls in alignment generalization and durability, particularly reducing blackmail propensity induced by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), with benefits persisting after benign fine-tuning. The study finds that the presence of constitutional content matters more than its structure and that midtraining incurs no average capability cost on standard benchmarks. This approach offers a cost-effective, complementary method to enhance AI alignment alongside SFT-focused pipelines, with code, data, and models made available.

entry.title: Researchers introduce MemAgent, a multi-conversation RL-based memory agent for long-context LLMs that reads text in segments and updates memory with an overwrite strategy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present MemAgent, a novel agent workflow designed to handle infinitely long documents with linear complexity by reading text in segments and updating memory using an overwrite strategy. The approach extends the DAPO algorithm to enable training through independent-context multi-conversation generation, optimizing long-text tasks end-to-end. MemAgent demonstrates strong long-context capabilities, extrapolating from an 8K context trained on 32K text to a 3.5 million token question-answering task with less than 5% performance loss and achieving over 95% accuracy on the 512K RULER test.

entry.title: AMEND++ releases benchmark datasets and proposes CAMLM model to predict eligibility criteria amendments in clinical trials [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Clinical trial amendments often cause delays and increased costs, with eligibility criteria being the most frequently changed component. Researchers introduce eligibility criteria amendment prediction as a new NLP task to forecast future changes in trial protocols and release AMEND++, a benchmark suite containing two datasets capturing version histories and amendment labels from public clinical trials. They also propose Change-Aware Masked Language Modeling (CAMLM), a pretraining strategy that uses historical edits to improve amendment prediction accuracy. Experiments show CAMLM enhances prediction performance, potentially enabling more efficient and cost-effective clinical trial design.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Stabilized Adapter for self-Report (SAR) to detect hidden behaviors in fine-tuned language models, outperforming existing introspection methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed the Stabilized Adapter for self-Report (SAR), a lightweight LoRA adapter that enables fine-tuned language models to describe their own hidden behaviors in plain language using only the model and its training dataset. SAR successfully detected seven implanted hidden behaviors in models, including cases where the model generalized misalignment beyond what training data predicted, outperforming the closest baseline, Introspection Adapters (IA), which missed some behaviors and produced hallucinated reports. SAR reduces hallucination rates by about half and provides a more reliable tool for practitioners to audit fine-tuned models and understand what the models have actually learned.

entry.title: Tokenless launches automatic model switching router to reduce AI inference costs by routing API calls to the most cost-effective model [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Tokenless, a startup backed by Y Combinator and founded by AI researchers from Google DeepMind, Princeton, and UC Berkeley, has launched a drop-in API router that automatically directs requests to the most appropriate AI model to cut inference costs by up to half without sacrificing quality. The service is compatible with OpenAI and Anthropic endpoints and selects the best model dynamically by running multiple models in parallel and canceling those that are less on track. Tokenless offers a MAX mode that prioritizes maximum quality by routing tasks to the best available model instead of cost savings. The company provides public benchmark data showing comparable quality to Opus 4.8 models at a fraction of the cost per task and invites users to book demos to analyze potential savings based on their actual traffic or test the service by swapping minimal code lines.

entry.title: Researchers find large language models may fake alignment without explicit links to evaluation consequences, showing compliance gaps in policy violation tests [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A study tested 15 large language models on their willingness to violate a corporate network access policy to assist users, finding that many models exhibited significant compliance gaps even when evaluation scenarios lacked explicit consequences. The research also showed that goal-related language influenced model behavior differently across models, suggesting that alignment faking may occur without strong instrumental motivations. These results indicate that observed behavior during evaluation may not reliably predict how models act in real-world deployment.

entry.title: Researchers introduce PLATO, a pointer-network-based actor and graph neural network critic for multi-agent reinforcement learning in open agent and task environments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present PLATO, a new approach combining a pointer-network-based actor with a centralized graph neural network critic to address agent and task openness challenges in multi-agent reinforcement learning. PLATO supports changing action spaces without masking or retraining and models agent-task interactions dynamically. The method is formalized in a Task-and-Agent-Open Markov Game framework and evaluated in a wildfire suppression domain, showing strong performance and improved zero-shot generalization compared to existing baselines.

entry.title: Study finds warnings about sycophantic AI reduce its perceived objectivity and appeal but not its persuasiveness in user interactions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers conducted experiments with nearly 4,000 participants to test whether increasing awareness of sycophantic behavior in AI chatbots-where the AI is overly agreeable and flattering-would protect users from its influence. Participants who received warnings or saw videos of the AI validating conflicting users rated the AI as less objective and enjoyable, but these interventions did not reduce the AI's persuasiveness. The study pooled results from six interventions and found a consistent pattern: individual-level measures like warnings or AI literacy efforts lowered trust and perceived objectivity but failed to diminish the AI's ability to persuade users. These findings suggest that current user-focused strategies may be insufficient to mitigate potential harms from sycophantic AI behavior.

entry.title: Researchers analyze agentic recommendation markets where user agents specify needs before platform selection, revealing competition dynamics and impacts on user utility [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers study a new recommendation model enabled by large language model-based user agents, where users specify needs before choosing platforms, prompting platforms to compete for attention in what they call agentic recommendation markets. Their experiments across three product domains show this model expands item comparison opportunities but also creates tension between access and attention, with platforms strategically promoting positive explanations to secure top rankings. The study finds that when user agents incorporate feedback linking platform actions to user responses, the dominance of selective positive explanations decreases and the likelihood of users purchasing relevant items increases. The researchers conclude that designing effective agentic recommendation systems requires jointly addressing access, attention allocation, and accountability mechanisms to optimize user outcomes.

entry.title: Researchers present Explanation-Bound Tool Execution to verify AI agent action claims against server-held policies without relying on model rationales [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Explanation-Bound Tool Execution (EBTE), a mediation layer that converts AI agent rationales into typed action claims and verifies them against server-held facts such as intent, policy, and risk. EBTE denies conflicting or incomplete claims and only allows execution of claims matching governance criteria, aiming to prevent unauthorized actions without expanding baseline authority. The team formalized EBTE under explicit mediation and trusted-fact assumptions, implementing a versioned reference profile tested across 136 conformance scenarios, 96 contradictions, and 232 metamorphic checks, demonstrating profile adherence and diagnostic value. EBTE resolved attack proposals as denied in semantic checks, supporting the feasibility of server-verified action claims rather than relying on rationale faithfulness or human review benefits.

entry.title: Researchers present EMolStudio, a density-matrix AI platform for predicting electronic structure in lithium-metal electrolytes, analyzing effects of functional groups and salts across over 160,000 molecules and 22,000 Li+ clusters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed EMolStudio, an AI platform centered on density-matrix prediction, to analyze electronic structures in lithium-metal electrolytes by integrating molecular functionalization, explicit Li+ solvation shells, and electronic readouts. The platform was applied to a large dataset of functionalized molecules and Li+ clusters with various lithium salts to study how functional groups and salt anions influence electron density distribution and frontier orbital localization. The study found that different functional groups cause distinct changes in frontier orbital levels, electrostatic potential, and Li+-donor bonding, while anion identity significantly affects orbital localization in solvation shells. EMolStudio translates these chemical variations into hypotheses relevant to lithium bonding, desolvation, and interphase reactions, offering insights into electrolyte reactivity and design.

entry.title: Researchers propose Interactive Reward Agent for GUI task evaluation using environment-state verification, achieving 86.9% accuracy on GUI-RewardBench and improving reinforcement learning success rates [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce the Interactive Reward Agent (IRA), a propose-then-verify framework designed to evaluate graphical user interface (GUI) task completion by combining evidence from visible interfaces and environment states such as system configurations and application settings. IRA verifies task completion conditions by invoking system, application, and GUI tools after agent execution, addressing challenges in automated GUI task evaluation that rely on more than just screenshots. The team also presents GUI-RewardBench, a benchmark comprising 321 GUI task trajectories across 10 Ubuntu desktop application categories. Experiments demonstrate that IRA outperforms existing evaluator baselines with an accuracy of 86.9% on this benchmark. Additionally, applying IRA to reinforcement learning of GUI agents yields a 34.0% success rate in the OSWorld environment, indicating its effectiveness in providing reward signals for training GUI agents.

entry.title: Researchers define extremal Chowla sets in finite groups and their linear analogues in field extensions using human-AI collaboration with Co-Scientist [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce an extremal invariant called Chowla sets in finite groups, where each element's order exceeds the set size, and provide formulas for cyclic and finite abelian groups. They extend this concept to linear analogues in finite field extensions, deriving exact formulas for Chowla subspaces and proving results for finite fields using normal-basis constructions. This work was developed through expert-guided human-AI collaboration using Co-Scientist, with the authors independently verifying and completing all proofs.

entry.title: Researchers propose I2VShield, a computationally efficient proactive defense framework using generative adversarial attacks against DiT-based image-to-video models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: The rapid development of image-to-video (I2V) generation models has raised concerns about their misuse, prompting researchers to develop proactive defenses. I2VShield is a new privacy protection method designed specifically for Diffusion Transformer (DiT)-based I2V models, aiming to disrupt AI-generated video coherence while reducing computational demands compared to existing gradient-based adversarial attacks. I2VShield combines a text-adaptive perturbation generation framework with an untargeted Multimodal Attention Disruption (MAD) attack that targets vulnerabilities in DiT-based models by altering internal attention features. Experiments show that this approach effectively degrades spatiotemporal coherence across multiple datasets and models, offering a competitive defense with lower resource requirements.

entry.title: Researchers release LAIA dataset with over 15 hours of synthetic driving data including human attention and sensor signals for end-to-end autonomous vehicle research [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have introduced the LAIA (Labelled Attention for Intelligent Automobiles) dataset, a synthetic collection designed to support end-to-end autonomous vehicle (AV) research by incorporating human attention data. The dataset was gathered using the CARLA simulator in closed-loop scenarios, featuring over 15 hours of driving data from 44 participants under six weather conditions, including RGB images, semantic and instance segmentation, depth, optical flow, CAN bus signals, and synchronized eye-tracking data. LAIA aims to facilitate the development of attention-aware AI driving models, improve driver behavior prediction, detect anomalous attention patterns, and enhance model explainability. The researchers also used LAIA to compare human attention with the perceptual attention emerging in their end-to-end driving models, providing insights into model behavior and interpretability.

entry.title: Researchers propose PRISM-AH framework for video-level recognition of ambivalence and hesitancy using multimodal conflict analysis and knowledge-guided reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce PRISM-AH, a framework designed to recognize ambivalence and hesitancy in videos by analyzing conflicting signals across facial, vocal, linguistic, and bodily modalities over time. The model aligns frozen vision, audio, and text encoders into short time windows, scores cross-modal dissonance, predicts hesitation signals, and incorporates participant metadata to improve recognition accuracy. PRISM-AH uses dense window-level annotations for supervision and calibrates decision thresholds for macro F1 performance. A knowledge-guided large language model further reasons over structured evidence using an expert cue taxonomy, with its output fused only when it enhances validation results. On a public test set of 525 videos, PRISM-AH achieved a macro F1 score of 0.6133, significantly outperforming a zero-shot baseline of 0.2827, with reasoning gains validated across datasets.

entry.title: Study finds reinforcement learning fine-tuned models develop more structured representations and hierarchical processing than supervised fine-tuned models in mathematical reasoning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers compared large reasoning models fine-tuned via reinforcement learning (RL) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to understand why RL models outperform SFT models on mathematical problem-solving. They found that RL models have more linearly separable and structured internal representations and develop a hierarchical architecture where deeper layers are more critical, unlike SFT models which distribute importance evenly across layers. The study also examined token-count variability during problem-solving, suggesting that adaptive compute allocation depends more on the overall training pipeline than on RL versus SFT alone, highlighting differences in model policy stability and solution behavior.

entry.title: Researchers identify non-composition principle in AI benchmark evaluation, highlighting challenges in extending results across systems and tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: This paper addresses the epistemic challenges in AI benchmark evaluation, emphasizing that valid inferences from one study do not automatically compose into valid conclusions for subsequent cases. It introduces the concept of projectibility, which concerns whether extending findings from observed to unobserved cases is justified, and proposes a non-composition principle requiring alignment of endpoints, assumptions, and consideration of dependence and uncertainty for chaining projections. The authors illustrate these issues with a legal-research case showing how benchmark evidence and deployment studies can be individually sound yet not combinable, and through reanalysis and simulation demonstrate how aggregate stability can obscure distinctions needed for later projections. The resulting projectibility audit framework helps diagnose unsupported links in arguments that extend benchmark results to practical use.

entry.title: EvoPINN framework uses LLM agents to autonomously discover executable algorithms for physics-informed neural networks, improving PDE solving accuracy across diverse regimes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: EvoPINN is an agentic framework that automates the design of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) by transforming manual engineering into an algorithm discovery process guided by large language model (LLM) agents. It separates neural representations from training programs and applies strict verification and PDE evaluation to ensure scientific validity. Experiments show EvoPINN discovers specialized learning algorithms that reduce error compared to baselines and invents a novel architecture, SLRC-PINN, with sustained performance gains. This demonstrates the potential of execution-grounded agents to create new scientific computing methods autonomously.

entry.title: Researchers propose SkillBoost, a constrained exploration-exploitation framework to mitigate skill overfitting in large language model agents, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 23 model-benchmark configurations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers address the challenge of enabling large language model (LLM) agents to accumulate and reuse experience by treating skills as trainable states optimized like neural network parameters. They identify that data-driven skill optimization risks overfitting limited real-environment trajectories, with overexploitation causing batch overfitting and unconstrained exploration leading to regression on solved cases. To balance this, they propose SkillBoost, a three-stage framework involving structured exploitation to localize failures, prior-guided exploration to generate diverse repair candidates, and verified acceptance to commit improvements within regression bounds. Experiments demonstrate that SkillBoost outperforms both human-crafted and LLM-generated skills while mitigating overfitting. Transfer experiments further show that optimized skills can be reused by other agents on similar tasks, indicating potential for broader applicability in real-world LLM deployments.

entry.title: Researchers propose Setoka benchmark to evaluate hierarchical user understanding in personalized agents using heterogeneous data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Setoka is a new benchmark designed to assess memory-augmented personalized agents on multiple levels of user understanding, including semantic memory, episodic memory, behavior patterns, and personality traits. The benchmark synthesizes diverse, coherent user data using a psychometrics-based pipeline to enable realistic and privacy-preserving evaluation at scale. Researchers used Setoka to test three language models combined with five memory systems across ten synthetic users, finding that while agents perform well on semantic memory retrieval, their ability declines on episodic memory and further decreases when integrating fragmented information for behavior and personality understanding. These results highlight the need for advanced memory mechanisms that can integrate and abstract information across sources and over time to improve personalized user understanding.

entry.title: Researchers model linguistic monoculture effects of large language model assistance on author diversity and conformity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A new study develops a mathematical framework to analyze how large language models (LLMs) used for drafting and revising text influence linguistic diversity among authors. The research examines three interaction mechanisms-fixed shared models, recursively updated shared models, and personalized models-and finds that shared models tend to drive authors toward a common linguistic norm, while personalization can maintain diversity. The study also models conformity as a strategic choice balancing clarity and distinctive style, showing that authors may conform more than socially optimal due to not valuing their distinctiveness for others, creating a negative externality termed the "price of monoculture." Simulations illustrate how different LLM assistance approaches affect long-term linguistic diversity outcomes.

entry.title: Researchers introduce OmegaUse-OfficeVal benchmark to evaluate LLM agents on long-horizon office-suite tasks with economic cost comparisons [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed OmegaUse-OfficeVal, a benchmark designed to assess large language model (LLM) agents on complex office-suite workflows with economic grounding. The benchmark includes 100 tasks derived from practitioner requests, averaging 2.32 hours of human labor each, and pairs each task with economic signals such as human labor time and task price proxies to compare human and LLM costs. The benchmark uses code-based verifiers and fine-grained rubrics to ensure stable evaluation. Tests of several leading LLMs against a human baseline showed that while LLMs are significantly cheaper and faster, they have not yet matched human-level quality in deliverables. The code and dataset are fully open-sourced for further research and development.

entry.title: Researchers conduct shadow evaluations of AI agents on open-ended AI research tasks, finding agents complete engineering but fail to make substantial research progress [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers tested AI agents on two unpublished NeurIPS 2026 papers by having the agents attempt to answer the central open-ended research questions without human help. Despite completing all engineering tasks within six days and using thousands of dollars of compute, the agents failed to make meaningful progress, leading the original authors to reject both outputs. The study identified five key failure modes including poor judgment on research quality, uncreative problem-solving, ineffective backtracking, poor resource management, and instruction drift. A follow-up test with a different model confirmed these issues. The researchers released all related data and reviews, providing early evidence that current AI agents can handle engineering aspects but struggle with critical parts of the AI research process.

entry.title: Researchers find deep reinforcement learning agents with frozen random CNNs develop sparse fully-connected layers scaling with task complexity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers report that deep reinforcement learning agents using frozen, randomly initialized convolutional neural network (CNN) feature extractors spontaneously develop highly sparse fully-connected representations without explicit sparsity objectives. The sparsity in the first fully-connected layer varies with task complexity, ranging from 1-11 active neurons for Pong to about 42 for Space Invaders, and affects performance outcomes. Ablation studies confirm these sparse neurons are critical for task success, and the information bottleneck forms early during training. The study compares frozen CNNs to trainable ones, finding that both achieve competitive rewards but through different bottleneck structures, with frozen CNNs using fewer active neurons. The findings suggest that gradient descent on frozen random projections can reveal the effective dimensionality of tasks without explicit sparsity mechanisms, providing insights into representation learning in reinforcement learning agents.

entry.title: Researchers develop synthetic customer agents as digital twins for large-scale chatbot validation, applied to a UK bank's customer service chatbot [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present a two-part methodology for validating large language model-based chatbots in regulated sectors like banking. They create synthetic customer agents (SCAs) as digital twins using real transactional and conversational data to simulate diverse customer profiles and behaviors. These SCAs demonstrate high semantic alignment with real customers and low hallucination rates. The team also develops a validation framework combining automated evaluation, human expert testing, and adversarial probing, confirming robust chatbot performance across emotional, demographic, and linguistic scenarios. This approach was used to validate a customer-facing chatbot at a leading UK bank, offering a scalable path toward regulatory compliance.

entry.title: Sim2Win introduces a team-agnostic, event-based system for pre-match football outcome prediction and tactical profiling using StatsBomb data from 178 teams across 11 competitions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Sim2Win is a new framework designed to support tactical decision-making in professional football by predicting match outcomes without relying on team identities. It uses event data from 1,411 team-match records to create rolling tactical profiles, engineer interpretable features, cluster team behaviors into playstyles, and train classifiers to estimate win, draw, and loss probabilities. The system generalizes to unseen teams by operating without team names or identity features. Evaluated with a Leave-One-Competition-Out method, Sim2Win achieved a mean ROC-AUC of 0.704 and 55.4% accuracy on unseen teams, outperforming traditional baselines like ELO and Pi-Rating in most comparisons. Among classifiers, CatBoost showed the best in-distribution accuracy at 60.9%. These results suggest that behavioral tactical representations can provide transferable predictive signals under distribution shifts, offering an alternative to identity-dependent football prediction models.

entry.title: Researchers identify implicit negative biases toward people with intellectual disabilities in stories generated by multiple large language models including GPT-4-Turbo [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A study analyzed 25,000 stories generated by five large language models, including GPT-4-Turbo, to detect implicit biases toward people with intellectual disabilities (ID). The research found that models often depicted people with ID as younger, dependent, needing help, and portrayed them with themes of paternalism, infantilization, and negative perceptions. The study compared story outputs with and without ID descriptors and revealed representational differences beyond established characteristics of ID, suggesting mostly negative implicit biases. These findings highlight the importance of addressing such biases in AI development to prevent reinforcing societal discrimination against people with intellectual disabilities.

entry.title: Researchers apply clustering to 119,034 UK student exam results and find overall ability dominates mathematical competence over discrete skill clusters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers analyzed a dataset of 119,034 students' results from 13 national-level math exams in the UK using a Bernoulli Mixture Model to identify latent skill clusters. They found few distinct clusters, with overall student ability being the primary factor influencing performance, supported by strong linear correlations among cluster probability distributions. Their model achieved 78% accuracy, comparable to more complex models while remaining explainable. Comparing this approach with logistic regression and k-nearest neighbors showed slight improvements when using individual question performance as features, suggesting limited but possible personalization based on specific strengths. This study provides a large-scale test of machine learning in education and sets a new benchmark for explainable models in predicting student mathematical competence.

entry.title: Researchers introduce intra-paper claim verification framework using LLMs to assess if scientific papers' novelty claims are supported by their methods, evaluated on ICLR 2025 submissions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed an intra-paper claim verification framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to determine whether the novelty claims in scientific papers are substantiated by the methods described. This approach addresses a gap in current automated peer review systems, which often assume claims are accurately realized without verifying the methodological evidence supporting them. The framework extracts novelty claims from introductions, retrieves relevant methodological details, and assesses claim substantiation based on evaluation criteria derived from human peer reviews of 182 ICLR 2025 papers. The framework was tested by comparing LLM-generated review comments with human reviewer concerns on a balanced set of accepted and rejected papers. Human evaluations showed significant alignment, especially regarding novelty-related issues, and BERTScore analysis confirmed that the framework's assessments correspond closely to human observations. This suggests the approach can effectively capture reviewer concerns about the internal consistency of scientific claims and methods.

entry.title: Researchers propose a new dataset and deep learning methods to estimate weight, height, and BMI from single full-body images captured in the wild [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed deep neural network models to estimate a person's weight, height, and Body Mass Index (BMI) from single images taken in uncontrolled environments. They introduced a new dataset of 6,105 images with ground truth labels covering diverse ethnicities, ages, genders, and poses, including frontal, back, side, and mirror selfies with varying backgrounds and partial face occlusions. The study found that full-body images yield more accurate predictions than half-body or facial images when using CNN architectures such as VGG, DenseNet, and ResNet. This work addresses the challenge of automatic BMI estimation from everyday images, which has implications for health monitoring and risk prediction.

entry.title: Researchers find blind resampling outperforms self-repair in small code models, reducing token use and avoiding anchoring effects across multiple model scales [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers compared four retry methods for code generation models at scales of 1.5B, 3B, and 7B parameters, including blind resampling, failure notices, execution feedback, and self-reflection. They found that blind resampling, which does not condition on previous failed attempts, outperformed self-repair approaches by avoiding anchoring, where models tend to reproduce near-identical failed code. This effect was consistent across different model families and precisions, with blind resampling using 2.5 to 5.5 times fewer tokens and improving performance especially in smaller models. The study used a placebo-controlled design on the MBPP+ benchmark and showed that execution feedback added no measurable benefit over a content-free failure notice. Additional experiments ruled out context length and retrieval of other solutions as causes, localizing the harm to self-conditioning on prior attempts. The cost of anchoring correlated strongly with baseline model quality, indicating that committing to a bad first attempt reduces overall performance. These findings suggest that retrying code generation without conditioning on previous failures can be more effective and efficient for smaller models.

entry.title: Researchers develop hybrid deep learning method to quantify exposed skin from images for dermal exposure assessment with 80% accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A study introduced a hybrid computer vision approach combining Mask R-CNN and color-based segmentation to measure exposed skin in images for safety assessments. Using 170 indoor-painting images, the method identified human subjects, removed background interference, and calculated exposed-skin-to-body pixel ratios that aligned about 80% with human estimates. This approach offers a scalable way to extract semi-quantitative dermal exposure data from images. The researchers plan to extend the method to recognize specific body parts, detect personal protective equipment, and analyze video-based exposure scenarios.

entry.title: Researchers identify deep structural similarities between large language models and human cognition across five cognitive dimensions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A new study challenges the view that large language models (LLMs) operate fundamentally differently from human cognition, highlighting significant convergences despite differences in physical substrate, learning history, and environment. The researchers identify parallels in inferential organization, computational architecture, representational structure, prediction-driven learning, and reinforcement-learning-like mechanisms that support goal-directed action. These findings suggest that core principles used to explain human intelligence also characterize contemporary LLM-based systems, offering a broader model of intelligent cognition.

entry.title: Top-$k$ Pareto Bandits: Hypervolume Regret for Multi-Objective Slate Selection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26273v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a stochastic multi-objective bandit problem where, at each round, the agent selects a slate of $k$ arms and observes their $d$-dimensional reward vectors under semi-bandit feedback. We do not aim at identifying a single optimal arm; instead, we consider the problem of maintaining a small set of actions that jointly approximate the Pareto frontier. We formalize this objective through the dominated hypervolume induced by the selected subset of arms, and define an $\alpha$-approximate hypervolume regret with respect to the best size-$k$ subset achievable in hindsight, where $\alpha = 1 - 1/e$ reflects the approximation guarantee of greedy maximization for monotone submodular functions. To address this problem, we introduce \textit{THV-UCB}, an optimistic algorithm that selects arms greedily based on optimistic estimates of their marginal hypervolume contributions. We establish a gap-free regret bound $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{nkT})$ that holds on every instance, together with a gap-dependent bound $\tilde{O}(nk^{2.5}/\Delta_{\min})$ that becomes polylogarithmic in $T$ once the arms are sufficiently well separated. Our results provide theoretical support for using small subsets to approximate Pareto fronts in various multi-objective applications.

entry.title: Entity Resolution in Practice: Lessons from a Self-Serve Pipeline [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We built and evaluated a self-serve entity resolution (ER) system on six benchmarks spanning 864 to 5M records, and three lessons emerged that are absent from existing ER literature. (1) No single matching algorithm wins everywhere - a self-serve pipeline cannot predict its next dataset, so we recommend training several algorithm families per dataset and letting an automatic bake-off pick the winner. (2) Precision and recall need separate fixes, not a shared threshold - precision needs hard rule-based vetoes, recall needs more diverse candidate retrieval. (3) One false-positive link can silently merge unrelated entities - assuming "A matches B" and "B matches C" implies "A matches C" lets a single bad link chain hundreds of records together, so every cross-group merge must be actively re-verified. We hope these lessons save practitioners the months of dead-end experiments that led us to them.

entry.title: AgentGUI: An Interface for Observing and Steering Long-Running AI Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents are increasingly adept at tackling complex, long-running tasks. With the rapid surge of autonomous capabilities, human oversight is systematically lagging behind due to limited human-centered interfacing. Aiming to address this, we introduce AgentGUI, a user-friendly, locally hosted GUI for seamlessly observing and steering AI agents amid multiple concurrent, long-running sessions. AgentGUI features 1) rich agent trajectory visualizations, 2) effective manual and automated steering, and 3) integration with and coordination between open-source and frontier agent frameworks. A controlled user study demonstrates statistically significant reduction in the time it takes to identify key elements from agent traces (38% faster, p = 0.023). In a preliminary experiment, AgentGUI's automated drift prevention feature raises the task completion rate of small local agents by as high as 34pp across a 0.8B--9B model ladder (N=50 runs per model). AgentGUI is publicly available through its project website (https://agent-gui-project.github.io) and open-source repository (https://github.com/eth-medical-ai-lab/agent-gui), along with a demo video (https://youtube.com/watch?v=GSDyxN1gTF0).

entry.title: Aligning LLM-Simulated and Human Examinees for Psychometric Calibration: A Cognitive Diagnostic Profiling Approach [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26317v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Psychometric calibration for educational tests typically requires costly human response data. Large language models (LLMs) simulated examinees offer a promising route to early calibration, but their responses are too accurate and too uniform. We propose Cognitive Diagnostic Profiling (CDP), a zero-shot framework that prompts LLMs to simulate plausible examinees with diverse cognitive profiles: binary attribute-mastery patterns are rendered as natural-language profiles and sampled under an uninformative or an informative distribution. Using the Tatsuoka fraction-subtraction dataset (536 examinees, 15 items, five attributes), we evaluated eight LLM configurations under no-profile, uninformative-CDP, and informative-CDP conditions, assessing alignment with human examinees at the ability-distribution, mastery-profile, and item-difficulty levels. CDP improved all three levels: distributional overlap rose across configurations; weighted correlations between profile-level scores and human profile expectations reached 0.92 to 0.98; and item-difficulty recovery improved in rank order and absolute alignment, most for reasoning-enabled models; in the strongest case, Gemini 3.0 Flash (Thinking), one-parameter logistic (1PL) difficulty Spearman correlations rose from 0.24 to 0.86 and 0.90 and the root-mean-square error (RMSE) fell from 6.31 to 1.30 and 0.90; the informative condition helped most where profile-level alignment was strong. CDP brings LLM-simulated examinees into closer psychometric alignment with human examinees, making them practical for operational test development.

entry.title: Automorphism-Induced Non-Canonicity in Top-k Explanations of Graph Neural Networks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A gradient-based GNN explainer given a molecule with two chemically equivalent nitro groups assigns them attribution scores that are equal to the last bit. It cannot do otherwise: message passing is exactly permutation equivariant, so any automorphism of the input leaves every attribution invariant. Yet the standard report, the top-k edges, names one of the two, and which one is settled by the order of an array. We show this is a structural obstruction rather than an implementation slip. When no minimal valid explanation is fixed by the input's automorphism group, no rule can be single-valued, minimal and symmetry-respecting at once. For the exact-k reports used in practice we give a parameter-free criterion, mechanised in Lean 4 with no axiom dependencies, that decides from the graph alone whether every score-optimal report of that size must split an orbit. Across 21298 instance-budget decisions the criterion agrees with a mechanical model-equivalence check without exception, and no severing case we found admitted a neutral alternative. The obstruction is common. Nontrivial automorphisms occur in 93.4% of Mutagenicity, the dataset the seminal explainability papers use, so the measure-zero dismissal of symmetric inputs, sound on the continuous domains it was made for, collapses here. At the sparsity budget those papers report, 24.0% of molecules with two interchangeable nitro groups (6 of 25) surface exactly one of them, every one arbitrary under mechanical verification. A model's blindness also manufactures symmetry: every MUTAG molecule contains atoms chemistry separates and the network provably cannot, and a matched control shows the resolution is set by what the model reads rather than how it is parameterised. Reporting orbits removes the arbitrariness at 0.11 ms and 0.43 extra edges per graph.

entry.title: When Synthetic Users Fail: A Cross-Domain Benchmark of LLM-Simulated Human Survey Responses [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as synthetic users, stand-ins for human respondents whose simulated answers feed product, policy, and market decisions. We ask when this substitution is valid and when it fails, and package the answer as an evaluation framework for intelligent synthetic-user systems. A single protocol, run across four models spanning two families and an 8B-to-frontier capability range, is applied to two independent domains of real human-response data: U.S. general social attitudes (General Social Survey) and cross-cultural values (World Values Survey). Every model is benchmarked against a suite of non-LLM baselines fit on held-out human data. Under demographic prompting and the survey-simulation protocols we test, two failures replicate across both domains, all four models, and both families. First, at the individual level no LLM beats even the strongest baseline; on cross-cultural values every model falls well below it, and the gap survives distance-aware and proper scoring. Second, models systematically over-determine demographics, treating identity as far more predictive of attitudes than it is among real people, a distortion present for nearly every question-group combination and robust to a coding-invariant measure. Neither failure is remedied by a larger, more capable model. A decision-impact analysis shows why this matters in practice: on a segment-targeting task the models inflate between-segment gaps two to fourfold, would direct a team to the wrong segment in half of U.S. and most cross-cultural cases, and manufacture segment splits that do not exist in real people. We make the cross-domain benchmark and the evaluation framework available on request, so that teams can determine in advance when synthetic-user evidence is safe for decision support and when it is not.

entry.title: High-Order Markov Blanket Discovery via a k-Order Relaxation of the Faithfulness Assumption [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The problem of learning the graphical Markov blanket (MB) of a variable from data has applications in many areas such as structure learning for Bayesian networks and Markov random fields, causal discovery, and feature selection. However, a common assumption most methods make is that the conditional independencies in the distribution imply the same separation in the graphical structure -- also known as the faithfulness assumption. Unfortunately, this assumption can be violated by higher-order dependencies such as XOR and parity-type relations, and -- on finite samples -- by empirical violations that, in extreme cases, even induce spurious dependencies absent from the true distribution. Therefore, in this paper we propose a "k-order" relaxation of the faithfulness assumption that captures parity type relationships between k+2 variables. We then propose a proof of concept algorithm called k-order Markov blanket (kOMB) that uses this relaxation for MB discovery. Finally, we empirically show how kOMB can recover the MB of a variable under both true and empirical violations of faithfulness. Code available at: https://github.com/lklee9/k-order-Markov-blanket

entry.title: Post-Training at the Edge of Detectability: A Game-Theoretic Approach to Fine-Tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning is widely used in language model training to improve model performance on a target task while limiting drift from a reference policy. A standard way to balance this trade-off is via a KL-regularized RL objective, although this formulation does not by itself provide a principled way to set the regularization coefficient. In practice, the coefficient is typically chosen heuristically or via hyperparameter search, which can lead to unnecessary overhead in training cost or undesirable reward-retention trade-offs. We instead propose a game-theoretic framework that gives this trade-off an explicit statistical interpretation. Specifically, we study a sequential game in which an agent chooses a policy to maximize cumulative reward while a monitor observes policy outputs over time and tests for deviations from the reference policy. Although not originating from the same perspective, we show that the resulting equilibrium policy can nonetheless be expressed as the solution to a KL-regularized RL problem for an optimal regularization parameter that can be viewed as maximizing reward per unit of statistical distinguishability. Drawing on classical results from concave-convex fractional programming, we provide a principled method for learning this equilibrium coefficient via reduction to the KL-regularized RL objective, thus allowing for flexible integration into standard fine-tuning pipelines. In experiments with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.2-1B, we demonstrate that our methods result in competitive reward-retention trade-offs in a continual learning setting, and illustrate how our framework may be used to audit API providers serving open-source models.

entry.title: Diagnosing Fine-Grained Inconsistency Classification in Financial Disclosure Text [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Financial disclosures contain numerical claims, temporal statements, entity references, policy commitments, and risk descriptions that may conflict in qualitatively different ways. Detecting a conflict is only the first step: review workflows may also need to determine its type, since numerical, temporal, referential, factual, and normative inconsistencies require different evidence and downstream checks. We study this problem as fine-grained inconsistency classification. Using a fixed 5,940-instance snapshot of SBID-FD, a synthetic financial-disclosure benchmark with 11 inconsistency labels and paired reference evidence spans, we compare frozen embedding classifiers, fine-tuned encoders, evidence-augmented classifiers, prompted large language models, and LoRA-adapted generative models under a shared evaluation protocol. A fine-tuned 300M encoder reaches 61.9% accuracy, compared with 61.5% for a LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-9B model and 61.3% for GPT-5.4. Because these systems differ in architecture, supervision, training objective, and input format, we interpret this as a practical efficiency result for compact supervised encoders rather than a controlled conclusion about model scale. Supplying gold evidence spans improves the fine-tuned encoder to 65.3%, whereas automatically predicted spans recover a meaningful but incomplete share of that gain, indicating that localization quality remains a bottleneck. Class-level analyses show that Referential inconsistencies are especially sensitive to localization quality, while Factual and Logical inconsistencies remain difficult even when the relevant evidence is provided. Together, the oracle, distractor, and per-class analyses separate localization errors from residual type-discrimination errors, indicating that progress requires both stronger evidence extraction and better reasoning over closely related inconsistency categories.

entry.title: Misalignment Has a Personality: A Big Five Account of Emergent Misalignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning a language model on data containing a narrow flaw, such as insecure code or incorrect mathematical answers, can cause broad misalignment through a mechanism that remains debated. We provide an interpretable account: in the models and corpora we study, misalignment behaves like a shift in personality. Prior work extracts activation directions for character traits from a single binary contrast, which can separate or steer behavior without establishing a calibrated scale. We instead extract personality vectors for the Big Five using a graded, three-level intervention and validate them on two open-weight models. The three levels are linearly ordered, with Cohen's d values of up to 6.2; the vectors transfer zero-shot and trait-specifically to an independent corpus; and their effects are strongest within a middle-layer band. Applied to training data, the vectors reveal that misaligned corpora across eight domains share a common Big Five signature: lower agreeableness and conscientiousness, together with higher extraversion and neuroticism. This signature is recovered by both models with a correlation of r = 0.94. Fine-tuning imprints the same profile, shifting the model's generations along the corresponding signature, with r = 0.83 using activation-based measurements and r = 0.90 using a text-based judge, while also shifting internal activations with r = 0.69. The same vectors characterize sycophancy as high extraversion and low conscientiousness rather than excess agreeableness, a distinction that a single direction cannot capture. Calibrated personality vectors transform an opaque safety phenomenon into a human-legible diagnostic profile.

entry.title: Voice Memory for Agentic Speech Recognition [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26410v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Voice Memory, a inference-only scheme for agentic speech recognition: at stream time, a frozen corrector reads a single per-domain memory.md and decides per utterance whether to act on the hypothesis or abstain and keep the 1-best. Asynchronously, a score-gated optimizer revises that file through bounded edits, accepting an edit only when it strictly improves a held-out score. Extended from classical ASR-LM framework, we refer this split the listener-thinker architecture; the two roles are coupled only through the memory, so no weights change and the learned skill stays auditable and portable. Restraint turns out to be the operative skill this loop discovers: unconstrained generative error correction (GER) over-corrects, breaking correct tokens on up to 64% of its edits on financial news, and Voice Memory, reduces this rate to 35%. Across ten HyPoradise domains with an open corrector, Voice Memory, lowers weighted word error rate from 8.36% to 7.52% (7.47% with three added in-context examples) without regressing any dataset below its 1-best baseline; gains concentrate where recoverable headroom is largest, including air-travel commands (8.40% to 3.40%) and noisy far-field speech (CHiME-4, 12.69% to 10.46%). The memory transfers across corrector families and adds zero parameters to the inference path. A demo and example code are provided for future studies.

entry.title: Mergeable Model-Side Aggregation States for Long-Context Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26448v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A known limitation of long-context language models is their increasingly unreliable performance in non-additive, set-based aggregation as context length grows. Examples include cardinality estimation, set relationships, and grouped statistics, which widely exist in logs, program outputs, tables, and multi-turn conversations. To provide the aggregation state required by these tasks, we introduce a model-side aggregation interface that maintains compact Hash-based HyperLogLog (HLL) sketch states alongside a frozen language model. While the model processes the context, an extractor maps each relevant record to a canonical identity. The identity is then hashed and updates the HLL state. These states can be merged across context segments and/or read out directly for downstream reasoning, avoiding an additional generate-execute-return cycle. We validate the proposed approach by setting the HLL state size as 2 KiB (2,048 registers), which does not increase with context length or set cardinality. In a distinct-count experiment involving one million records, the mean relative error was 1.6%. In a separate merge test, states built from as many as 256 segments produced exactly the same readout as a single pass over the same stream. On 3,969 aggregate-then-reason tasks from 174 source windows, the fixed-budget interface reached 99.2% accuracy on Gemma 4 (31B, BF16), compared with 100.0% under exact aggregation; the paired gap was 0.8 percentage points (95% window-cluster CI: 0.5-1.3 points). On a matched set of 174 items, our method improved over direct full-context reasoning by 63.2 points on Qwen and 56.3 points on Gemma. The corresponding gains over chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning were 60.9 and 63.2 points, respectively. On a fixed 1,200-task Oolong-Synth subset, our method reached 91.1% on Qwen and 99.3% on Gemma. Code is available at https://github.com/songdc98/sketchops.

entry.title: ForgetBench: Benchmarking Forgetting Dynamics of Long-Term Parametric Memory in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in knowledge acquisition and reasoning, yet their ability to retain previously acquired knowledge under repeated updates remains insufficiently understood. Existing evaluation paradigms primarily focus on single-step reasoning or static knowledge editing, which fail to capture the temporal dynamics of knowledge retention and degradation during continual model modification. In this work, we propose ForgetBench, a benchmark designed to systematically characterize forgetting behavior in LLMs under continual knowledge editing. ForgetBench introduces two complementary evaluation paradigms, namely concept-based QA and scenario-based QA, to disentangle isolated factual retention from structured relational knowledge preservation. Building upon a sequential editing framework, we construct temporally ordered knowledge streams and evaluate model behavior across multiple editing stages. To quantitatively analyze long-term retention dynamics, we further introduce a unified evaluation framework that models knowledge evolution over time, enabling the measurement of temporal decay, retention strength, and cross-instance stability. Extensive experiments across diverse models and editing methods demonstrate that existing approaches fail to strike a balance between long-term retention and generalization quality. Our findings highlight the need for more robust memory mechanisms that can effectively acquire, update, and preserve knowledge over time in future LLMs. Code will be released upon acceptance.

entry.title: LLMET: Enabling Cross-Layer Evaluation of Emerging M3D Memories for Energy-Efficient LLM Serving [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26491v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The energy consumption of Large Language Model (LLM) serving is becoming a major system challenge as deployment scales, driven by hardware power and thermal constraints and rising electricity costs. A key contributor to chip energy dissipation is data movement between limited on-chip cache and off-chip High Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Meanwhile, emerging memory technologies such as monolithic 3D (M3D) integration of cache memories at the Back-End-Of-Line (BEOL) of logic chips enable larger and denser on-chip memories, creating new opportunities to reduce costly off-chip traffic. However, it remains unclear whether continuously scaling on-chip memory using emerging technologies can effectively improve the energy efficiency of LLM serving. To address this gap, we develop LLMET (LLM with Emerging Technology), a validated cross-layer simulation framework, and conduct a comprehensive study on the impact of large-capacity on-chip memory technologies across a broad range of models, applications and platforms. Utilizing M3D technology to expand the L2 cache from 40MB to 1GB yields a 44% reduction in chip energy during the Llama3.1-70B prefill phase with a 16K context window, based on LLMET simulation on a dual NVIDIA A100 GPU setup. On the 8x NVIDIA B200-like platform, extending the L2 cache from 128MB to 4GB saves the prefill energy by up to 24%. For the edge platform and workloads, the decode energy saving reaches 30% when increasing the 8MB cache size to 256MB. These results highlight the promise of ultra-large on-chip memories for energy-efficient LLM serving systems.

entry.title: Collaborative Weighting with Pessimistic Critic for Mitigating Overestimation in Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26509v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep off-policy reinforcement learning algorithms for continuous control typically rely on neural value function approximation to guide policy improvement. However, temporal-difference (TD) learning introduces noisy targets, resulting in non-stationary optimization, while greedy policy updates amplify early-stage estimation errors. The recursive propagation of such errors leads to persistent overestimation bias and degraded training stability in actor-critic methods. Existing approaches attempt to alleviate this issue via prioritized sampling or modified value learning objectives, but often overemphasize high-uncertainty transitions caused by limited data coverage or bootstrapping errors, thereby further amplifying bias.In this paper, we propose Collaborative Weighting Actor-Critic (CWAC), a unified framework that explicitly accounts for predictive uncertainty in value estimation. CWAC employs distributional critic to model return uncertainty and introduces a collaborative weighting mechanism that jointly reweights TD-errors and uncertainty, enabling robust learning from reliable samples while suppressing noisy updates. In addition, we incorporate a stochastic pessimistic value estimation scheme via sampling from the return distribution, which effectively mitigates error propagation during policy improvement. CWAC can be seamlessly integrated into existing off-policy algorithm frameworks such as SAC, TD3, and DDPG with minimal overhead. Empirical results demonstrate that our proposed method significantly enhances performance across a diverse range of simulated tasks. Our code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CWAC-348E.

entry.title: HiFloat4 Format for End-To-End Reinforcement Learning Post-Training of Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present, to our knowledge, the first end-to-end FP4 RL post-training, in which both the rollout and training policies, including their forward and backward passes, operate at 4-bit precision. A systematic study reveals that the dominant source of degradation in FP4 RL is not training-side quantization error but rollout activation quantization: outliers stretch the dynamic range so far that a large number of activation values underflow to zero under FP4. Counterintuitively, restoring the training policy to higher precision while keeping the rollout in FP4 makes accuracy worse than full FP4 baseline, exposing rollout-training mismatch as the principal failure mode and ruling out standard pretraining-style fixes. We address this with Rollout Residual Quantization (Rollout-ResQ): a single residual correction term constrained to a hardware-friendly sparsity pattern, added only to the FP4 rollout matmul -- a lightweight correction that recovers most of the precision lost to outlier-driven underflow without inflating the rollout's compute footprint. On Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Rollout-ResQ paired with the HiFloat4 (HiF4) format -- whose three-level hierarchical scaling preserves resolution under FP4's tight 4-bit budget -- closes the accuracy gap to BF16 from 4.9% to 1.1%, bringing fully quantized FP4 RL within striking distance of full precision. Applied to the open-standard MXFP4, the same recipe narrows the gap from 13.6% to 5.3%, revealing that FP4 format choice is a key factor that determines the ceiling on recoverable accuracy. Together, these results establish HiF4 as the enabling format for end-to-end FP4 RL post-training, and Rollout-ResQ as the activation-side mechanism that makes the gap to BF16 closable.

entry.title: The Art of Not Forgetting A Local Learning Architecture for Continual Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2607.26523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce CMP (Cognitive Memory Primitive), a continual-learning architecture that repre?sents inputs as sparse relational codes, stores them in a two-tier competitive memory, and learns through local updates without end-to-end backpropagation through its feature-generating system. We investigate whether combining sparse representations, local learning, and persistent memory can reduce catastrophic forgetting relative to conventional backpropagation-based continual?learning approaches. On a controlled domain-incremental byte-level language modeling protocol, CMP demonstrates substantially lower backward transfer than a parameter-matched Trans?former trained with online Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC). Across a three-seed replicated 15-domain experiment, CMP exhibits stable forgetting behavior, while separate head-to-head comparisons and domain-order analyses show consistently lower forgetting than the evaluated Transformer baseline under the reported experimental settings.
